en: Annotated Praise to Amitāyus Buddha (with Preface).

The verses of praise composed by the Vinaya Master of Great Wisdom are concise in expression yet rich in meaning; their purport is vast and far-reaching. The Way of Mind-Only is fully realized herein.
I have often lamented that while the commentaries of our school’s two or three eminent masters circulate widely, people tend to grasp the meaning merely according to the literal words.
The ultimate aim is obscure; there seems to be something that suppresses the intent of the author, which is deeply regrettable.

Having encountered fellow practitioners of the Way, and considering that I, though foolish, have once studied the teachings of the Mountain School (Sanjia) and have superficially investigated this tradition, I was again commissioned to provide annotations. Although I am not gifted, my views differ from what has been heard before;
I have therefore gathered the aphorisms of the sutras and śāstras to directly expound its essential meaning, hoping that it may lead to a slight awakening regarding the journey toward the West.

This collection of provisions is not merely intended to purchase the reputation of surpassing one's teacher. Those who read it should take its principles as their standard of excellence, rather than taking its personal sentiments as such.
Written on the Mid-Autumn Day of the Gengwu year while residing at the Lanya Hermitage in Sanjiang.
In the *Commentary on the Praise of Amitāyus Buddha* by Zhu’an Jiedu:
"The annotation of the eighty-four thousand wondrous marks— could these not be the Amitābha of one's own original nature?"

The first phrase cites the merit of those fruits. In the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, it is stated that the primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*), as well as the radiance, each number eighty-four thousand.
Because the root subsumes the branches, only "marks" are mentioned here; this serves to indicate that the afflictions (*kleśa*) within the causal stage have been purified.
Therefore, the primary marks and secondary signs are numbered at eighty-four thousand. Sentient beings likewise possess such dharma-gates, yet it is only due to...
What was previously manifested as the afflictions (*kleśa*) becomes a supreme function once realized by the Buddhas. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states:
"The eighty-four thousand gates of the various afflictions cause sentient beings to become exhausted; yet the Buddhas perform the Buddha-work precisely through these very dharmas.
Furthermore, these marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) are all perfectly real and constitute the path-factors of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra-mārgāṅga*).
The arousal of what is cultivated is termed "wondrous. The second phrase points to the Buddha as being identical to nature; the merit of the fruition is lofty and profound.
One understands that sentient beings and Buddhas are not separate from a single kṣaṇa, sharing the same source of awakening.

Perfectly illuminating all phenomena, the present single thought-moment is itself the body of the Dharma-realm of all Buddhas, for all Tathāgatas have no realization apart from this—they fully realize the very nature of sentient beings.

There is an inherently present wondrous nature. The *Vajra-needle* states: "Therefore, we know that at the stage of fruition (*phala-bhūmi*), the environment and its inhabitants are interfused, for both depend upon the fundamental nature of the principle of sentient beings.
The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "Sentient beings are themselves the Buddha. Why? Because apart from sentient beings, one cannot attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The *Awakening of Faith* states: "That which is called the meaning of enlightenment refers to the substance of the mind..."
It is free from thought. That which is free from the marks of thought is equal to the realm of empty space, pervading everywhere without exception.
The single mark of the Dharma-realm is precisely the Tathāgata’s eternally abiding Dharmakāya. Based on this Dharmakāya, it is termed "original enlightenment" (prakṛti-awakening).

Thus one knows that the perfectly luminous essence of the Buddha of the fruition is the inherent nature-virtue possessed by us ordinary beings; it is entirely the support for the form and mind of sentient beings.
Correct. It has no separate essence. Since it completely constitutes my own mind, it manifests right where it is.

One need only observe that one’s own mind is itself the Buddha-body. Therefore, a sutra says: "When the mind contemplates the Buddha, this very mind is the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics;
this mind creates the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha. Furthermore, the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "The Buddha is my..."
The mind. It is my mind that sees the Buddha; it is my mind that creates the Buddha. The *Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra* states:
"With my Buddha-eye, I behold within all sentient beings—amidst their afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion—the wisdom of the Tathāgata, the eye of the Tathāgata, and the body of the Tathāgata.
Seated in the full lotus posture, majestic and unmoving, they are eternally undefiled and endowed with all virtuous marks."
It is sufficient. It is no different from my own [realization]. The *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states: "The liberation of all Buddhas should be sought within the mental activities of sentient beings.
This means that it manifests solely in dependence upon the mind and is not separate from True Suchness (*tathatā*). One observes the mind all day long; one observes the Buddha all day long.
The entire mind is the Buddha; the entire Buddha is the mind. This is truly because the entire dharma-realm constitutes my single thought-moment.
Furthermore, the entire body manifests as the body of Amitābha. Since both the Dharma-realm and the mind-Buddha are without distinction, they mutually interpenetrate in an inconceivable manner.
Not only is this true of the mind and the Buddha, but all phenomena are likewise so.

Thus, the two deaths, the five stages of dwelling, the hells, form and mind, the environment and its inhabitants, causes and effects—none of these in the mundane or supramundane realms are not the perfect fullness of the Dharma-realm.

The secret treasury of the three virtues is unified; it is solely because Amitābha realized this principle that he understood his own nature and practiced in accordance with it, thereby perfectly realizing the three bodies and manifesting the four pure lands.

Because all sentient beings are deluded regarding this principle, they turn their backs on their nature and practice in opposition to it, thus constantly dwelling within the three realms and remaining forever buried in the four miserable destinies.
Although they remain entirely in delusion, they have never for a moment deviated from what the Buddha has realized.

It is only because sentient beings do not know that the principle of the three obstacles is entirely Buddha that they give rise to delusions and create karma within this very principle, cycling through birth and death.
For long kalpas they employ this principle, yet for long kalpas they remain ignorant of it. It is not due to ignorance that they lose this principle;
the manifest fruits of suffering are themselves the Dharmakāya, and the dark obscurity of the three delusions is in its entirety the luminous illumination. Thus it is concluded.
The characteristics of karmic entanglements are all marks of liberation. Thus, Jingxi said: "Sentient beings, from time immemorial, have possessed nothing but afflictions, karma, and suffering;
these are entirely the three causes of the rational nature (*li-xing*). He further stated: "To speak briefly, the beginningless wheel of suffering is boundless;
it is neither identical with nor distinct from karma and afflictions," and so on, continuing until: "Therefore, the three paths and..."
Since these three virtues possess no sequence of before or after, the three causal natures of these virtues are never absent at any time.
This is to say that the three obstacles are entirely the ultimate fruit-function of all Buddhas.

Now that we have understood this principle, we must single-mindedly contemplate the environment and body of Amitābha, permeating our own mind-nature to manifest the essence of the True Buddha. Although we rely upon that objective realm, we must know that...
"The primary and secondary [realms] dwell together within one mind; since the mind is complete [in itself], how could that which arises be separate from the nature of mind?
If even a single hair's breadth of a dharma were seen as coming from without, it would not be the Mahāyāna contemplation of mind-only and phenomena.
Furthermore, although Amitābha Buddha alone is taken as the object, he already embodies all Buddhas; therefore, the Sūtra says: 'One who sees the Buddha of Infinite Life sees the ten directions.'"
Regarding the immeasurable Buddhas: it is because all Buddhas have equally realized the secret treasury of the three dharmas. The secret treasury of one Buddha is not small;
the secret treasury of all Buddhas is not many. To raise one is to encompass all; to perfect all is to be one. As the Sūtra says:
One body and one wisdom; the powers and fearlessnesses are likewise so.
The distant reaches of hundreds of thousands of billions of lands are, in truth, the Pure Land of the Mind alone.
The first phrase points to that Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*). As the Sūtra says: "From here, to the west, passing through hundreds of thousands of billions of Buddha-lands, there is..."
The world is named Sukhāvatī; this is precisely the Pure Land of Shared Dwelling that the Bhikṣu Dharmākara took as his vow during his causal stage.
Regarding the second phrase, "understanding that the land is solely mind": this is because the single mind manifest before us inherently possesses the three virtues.
It is named the "Eternally Quiescent Light. Its profound stillness and immobility are called "eternal" (*nitya*); its nature being fundamentally free from defilement is called "quiescent" (*śānta*);
and the luminous clarity of the *dharmadhātu* is called "light" (*prabhā*). This is entirely the essence of the "mind-only" (*cittamātra*).
Therefore, the Patriarch said: "The body and the land abide within a single mind. Thus, one knows that the essence of the mind is itself the Eternally Quiescent Light. Within this quiescent light...
The land is neither dual nor distinct; the body of Vairocana accords perfectly with his land. The Dharma-body, the Reward-body, and the Responsive-body are of one essence without differentiation.

It is further said: "The entire environment and its inhabitants of the Avīci hell reside within the self-mind of the Ultimate Sage; the body and land of Vairocana do not exceed the single thought-moment of an ordinary person below.
This is simply because the substance of the mind is fundamentally without intrinsic nature, manifesting through transformation in accordance with conditions."

The functions of the three lands arise [therefrom]. Therefore, although Amitābha dwells loftily in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang), which lies beyond a hundred thousand [yojanas] in a remote realm, it is entirely the land of the principle of tranquil light within my own mind.
As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "In the triple world there are no separate dharmas; they are all created by this one mind alone.
Thus, the Buddhas of the ten directions and all sentient beings of the past, present, and future, throughout the void...
Buddha-fields are fundamentally possessed by the mind alone; they arise entirely from the mind. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:

"The wondrous, enlightened, luminous mind pervades the worlds of the ten directions, containing and nurturing the pure, jewel-adorned lands of the Tathāgatas—the realms of the Wondrous Enlightened Kings. It further states:

"The empty space of the ten directions arises within your own mind, like a single fragment of cloud appearing in the vast clarity of the great sky. How much more so, then, [the case of] all [other phenomena]?
Does the world exist within empty space? If even one among you awakens to the truth and returns to the source, this emptiness of the ten directions will all vanish away.
This is because this mind is perfectly endowed with the three virtues, pervading the Dharma-realm and being identical to the eternally quiescent light.
There is not a single dharma that exists outside my mind; there is not a single dharma that is not the substance of my mind.
Therefore, the entire mind is the land, and the entire land is the mind. Since the mind has nothing external to it, how could there be a Pure Land suspended elsewhere in another direction?
If one can understand in this way, then one sees that land as being purely one's own mind and not some other realm.

Because one is constantly taking up the earth, cultivation arises entirely from the nature; thus it is not something spontaneous. Because one is constantly abiding in the mind-only, cultivation is itself the nature.
Thus, it is not dependent on causes and conditions; both cultivation and nature are simultaneously extinguished, and only the essence of mind is revealed.

Furthermore, one should know that the eighty thousand marks and signs constitute the supreme response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) of Amitābha. Once the original nature is realized, the three bodies are fully present and the four virtues are without deficiency;
this is precisely the wisdom of initial awakening (*ādikṣānti-jñāna*). The ten million billion lands are the Western Land of Common Dwelling (*sahā-loka-dhātu*).

If one realizes that there is only mind, this is precisely the serene light (*śāntaprabhāsa*), wherein there is no phenomenon that is not the Dharma-realm; this is the principle of original enlightenment (*mūla-avabodha*).
When initial enlightenment (*ādi-avabodha*) is perfected, original enlightenment is fully revealed. Initial and original enlightenment merge as one, with no further division.

Thus we know that apart from the body there is no land, and apart from the land there is no body. These are two meanings within a single reality. Why is this? The body also consists of the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*), and the land likewise consists of the three.
Virtue. Since both possess the three virtues and both are the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), the Dharma-realm has a single characteristic; there is no difference between body and land.

Furthermore, the land belongs to the "support" (*āśraya*) and the Buddha-body belongs to the "supported" (*adhiṣṭhāna*). Since support and supported both reside within one mind, how could that one mind be divided into subject and object?
Therefore, the body and land of Amitābha are not separate from my own mind. In a single thought-moment, the complete essence is perfectly realized as the Buddha.
The Pure Land of Mind-Only does not require seeking afar; the Amitābha of one's own nature is certainly not to be sought from without.

Only those who understand in this way truly accord with perfect cultivation. If one merely contemplates the environment and the body of that Responsive Buddha (nirmāṇakāya), how can it be called the Mind-Only or the Original Nature?
Although purity and defilement are separated, how could they transcend one’s own mind?
This steps upon the Pure Land of Mind-Only. Though it is said that the Pure Land is nothing but my own mind, alas, this mind is entirely defiled and stained.
That Buddha-land is pure, wondrous, and adorned; purity and defilement remain distinct. It rests solely upon the mind.
This should be understood as the conceptual construction of the discerning mind. If one realizes that there is only mind, how could purity and defilement exist?

This is because all lands, whether pure or defiled, are entirely the manifestation of the functional activity of the Dharma-realm of tranquil light (*śānta-prabhāsvara*). It is only because sentient beings, according to their capacities, falsely cling to them that purity and defilement are distinguished.
When one investigates the fundamental nature of phenomena, how could this be so? As stated in the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, when the Brahma King Śikhin reproached his own body...
The Master said: "Do not harbor such thoughts as to consider this Buddha-field impure. Why is this?
I see the land of Śākyamuni Buddha as pure, like the palace of the sovereign god (Īśvara).

It is because your minds, O virtuous ones, possess highs and lows and do not rely on the Buddha’s wisdom that you perceive this land as impure. He further said: "It follows the state of one's own mind..."
When there is purity, the Buddha-field is pure. By analogy, it may also be said: according to the defilement of the mind, the Buddha-field is defiled.
To be deluded regarding the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is called ignorance; this is termed "defilement. To realize that ignorance is itself the nature of phenomena is termed "purity.
This is a distinction between purity and defilement within a single principle. It is like clear water and turbid water, which, though different, share the same nature of moisture.

There is no distinction. Thus, the purity of the Land of Ultimate Bliss and the defilement of the Saha world, though separated by a distance of a hundred thousand worlds, are equally the Constantly Quiescent Light;

they are both entirely my own mind-nature. Since one knows that purity and defilement are wholly the mind-nature, and the mind-nature is fundamentally empty, there is no master over purity or defilement.
Vairocana pervades all places, and all dharmas are nothing other than [the Buddha].
Regarding Buddha-nature, how could purity and defilement be permitted to exist within it?
Although the sentient being and the Buddha differ, how could they ever deviate from their own nature?
This refers to the aforementioned original nature of Amitābha. Amitābha has already awakened and perfectly realized the three bodies (trikāya); sentient beings, however, remain lost in delusion.

Consequently, the three obstacles arise; delusion and awakening become separated, and one's own nature falls into discord. This is merely the clinging of the mind—what has it to do with the ultimate principle?
Within the realm of True Suchness (*tathatā*), the provisional names of "sentient beings" and "Buddhas" are extinguished; within the nature of equality, the forms of "self" and "other" do not exist.
The entirety of the three obstacles of sentient beings is itself the Principle; the three bodies (*trikāya*) of all Buddhas are none other than the inherent nature. Thus, throughout the world...

The intermediate characteristics are eternal; sentient beings are themselves Buddhas. Although they are deluded by the obscurations of views and thoughts, the underlying principle remains present therein.
If one knows that this mind is no different from the Buddha, then the Buddhas of the ten directions will all enter into one’s own mind. Thus, the *Golden Scalpel* says:
The fruit of Buddhahood possesses the causal nature of both self and others; my own mind possesses the resultant virtues of all Buddhas.

When viewed from the perspective of the Buddha-eye and Buddha-wisdom within the state of fruition, there is only the Buddha’s non-arising (*anutpāda*). Within the causal stage, if one’s true wisdom and true eye are in dark resonance with reality, then even this very arising is entirely the Buddha.
As the *Fenbie Ermen* (Gate of Non-duality) states: "If you simply recognize a single thought-moment, you will see everywhere the arising of both yourself and others."
The Buddha. If other beings and other Buddhas are already identical with the mind, how much more so must the Buddha born from one's own mind not diverge from it for even a single thought-moment?

This is because the mind alone is fundamentally complete; it is the mind that undergoes transformation and creation, and its entire substance gives rise to function. The principle of cause and effect is the same.
Only those who can understand this may be said to realize that there is no difference between mind, Buddha, and sentient beings.
The substance of the mind is vast and empty, unimpeded by coming and going; its nature is fundamentally all-encompassing, so what hindrance could there be to acceptance or rejection?
As for the mind and its nature, they may be distinguished as "true" and "delusive. As Jingxi said: "Following conditions without changing is called nature;
not changing while following conditions is called mind. In the present text, both mind and nature belong to the true; they are one essence with two names.
Listen. As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "The eternally abiding true mind, the essence of pure and luminous nature. It further states:
"The perfectly wondrous and luminous mind, the precious, luminous, and wondrous nature. Such is the essence of the mind-nature (*cittatā*): it is empty yet pervasive, quiescent yet illuminating;

its essence and nature are eternally abiding, its virtuous capacity is boundless, the three truths are perfectly interfused, and the one mind is fully present. Therefore, the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) says: "It is able to contemplate..."

The nature of the mind is called the supreme concentration (*adhi-samādhi*). That which is the supreme concentration is called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), is named Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), and is named Vairocana.
This very nature of Vairocana possesses the three Buddha-natures; because Vairocana is all-pervasive, Buddha-nature is likewise all-pervasive.
Therefore, we know that the three Buddhas are but a single *kṣaṇa*. Since the three Buddhas are all-pervasive, the *kṣaṇa* is itself pervasive.
This is the wondrous nature and wondrous mind of the Three Truths. "Vast and empty" describes its pervasive nature; this demonstrates the magnitude of its essence.

"Broad and great, fully complete," it is perfectly pervasive throughout all phenomena, having no fixed location or direction. As the *Jingangbei* says: "It is neither internal nor external; it pervades emptiness."
It is empty, identical to all Buddhas, and equal to the Dharma-realm; thus one knows that this mind pervades all places.

"Encompassing" refers to its nature being fully endowed [with all qualities]; this demonstrates the virtue of its essence (*tī*). Indeed, because this nature is fully endowed with all dharmas, it is itself all dharmas.
It encompasses myriad virtues and there is nothing it does not contain. Therefore, Jingxi said: "This pervasive nature is fully endowed with all Buddhas."
The body is the one body and all bodies; as the lands manifested by the Buddhas are one land and all lands, so too are body and land mutually identical.
The discourse on the body and the discourse on the land—whether large or small, one or many—are likewise thus. One thereby knows that this mind contains all phenomena.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "As one wishes, it can contain all worlds of the ten directions and the three periods of time."
Regarding mundane and supramundane phenomena, there is nothing that the Sage does not encompass within the ordinary person, exhausting their very limits.

This is truly because the mind is itself the Dharma, and the Dharma is itself the mind. A mustard seed constantly contains Mount Sumeru, and a mote of dust inherently includes the entire Dharma-realm;
this is because, in every instance, everything is entirely the nature of the mind. It is, for example, like a box and its lid containing other objects.

Is this not what is meant? Therefore, Tiantai said: "It contains and accommodates much, yet there is no accumulation. This refers to the principle of the *tathāgatagarbha*, wherein all phenomena are utterly extinguished;
yet while phenomena are extinguished, they still exist. Phenomena remain vividly present—eternally empty and eternally provisional, with both emptiness and illumination simultaneously realized.
Neither of the two extremes can be grasped, and even the Middle Way does not exist. This is Great Nirvāṇa, named the Secret Treasury.

If the nature of the mind is thus, how could there be defilement to be abandoned or purity to be attained? This is because the coming and going, the taking and rejecting, and the pure and impure bodies and lands are all the *dharmadhātu*;
they are precisely the wondrous mind and wondrous nature. The nature of the mind is profoundly still, devoid of even a single mark of difference.
Amitābha’s environment and its inhabitants are entirely one's own mind; how could one, by means of that very nature of the mind, further grasp at anything else?
The nature of the mind is like this: suppose there were a person who, wishing to avoid empty space, set out for another country; he would only increase his fatigue. How can one avoid space?

If that were possible, then though traveling back and forth all day, he would not have moved even a single step; though constantly grasping and discarding things all day, he would not have engaged in a single thought.
Furthermore, it should be known that coming and going, grasping and discarding, are dependently originated phenomena (*pratītyasamutpanna*). Dependently originated...
Since non-substantiality is utterly unobtainable, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "Phenomena born of causes and conditions are themselves emptiness, the provisional, and the middle.

It further states: "All phenomena are not produced from themselves, nor are they produced from another; they are not produced from both together, nor without cause; therefore, they are said to be unproduced.
Having realized the three truths and further transcended the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), one abandons the marks of coming and going as well as the mind of acceptance and rejection.
There is nowhere to rely upon. The *Ten Doubts Treatise* says: "The Wise One ardently seeks birth in the Pure Land, yet realizes that the essence of birth is unobtainable;
this is true non-arising (*anutpāda*). This is what is meant by: 'When the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure. The fool is bound by birth;

upon hearing of birth, he immediately forms a conceptualization of birth, and upon hearing of non-arising, he immediately forms a conceptualization of non-arising, not knowing [the true nature] of birth."

This is precisely non-arising; non-arising is itself arising. One who can understand it thus and cultivate progress in every thought-moment may attain the superior golden platform in a single lifetime.
Therefore, by raising a single thought, one immediately ascends to the Treasure Realm and returns to one's native home on earth, facing upward with a mere snap of the fingers.
Within this compassionate countenance, there is truly a reunion of the natural father and son.
Therefore, following the words of the Superior, a single thought-moment or the snap of a finger is used as a metaphor for its swiftness.
Regarding "returning," the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "It is like a person who travels far away on business; before they have returned, they already clearly know their home."

The path of returning is the ground of ultimate reality (dharmatā). The home is the home of the dharma-nature (dharmatā). "Heavenly and true" means natural and spontaneous. Regarding "father and son":
one is born into the family of the Tathāgata as a prince of the dharma. This may also be understood by taking a distant reference to the time of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū.
When Amitābha was one of the sixteen princes, he lectured on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* for his father;
thus, in examining their fundamental basis, they resided in the stage of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and dwelt within the household of Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), having long been father and son.

Yet, through a single delusion regarding their native land, father and son were suddenly estranged. Now that the land is understood to be mind-only and the Buddha is realized as being identical to nature, [they remain as such].
I shall not fail you. Whether lifting my foot or setting it down, how could I ever stray from my native land? Let this thought be ever present, for I am always close to my compassionate father.
For many lifetimes I have repaid your kindness with ingratitude and suffered in the depths of samsara; today, as I cast myself upon your mercy, may I surely receive your salvation.
The phrase "several lifetimes" refers to its beginninglessness; the expression "bearing a debt of virtue" speaks of the arising of delusion.

Originally endowed with the three virtues, one becomes confused and turns away from them, failing to realize them, and thus undergoes birth and death—this is to be guilty of violating the inherent nature and virtue of father and son. The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:

"All sentient beings, from time immemorial, have had their births and deaths succeed one another; this is entirely due to not knowing the eternally abiding true mind and its intrinsically pure nature."
The essence is clarity; its function consists of various deluded thoughts. Because these manifestations are not true, there is cyclic existence. It further states:
"Because sentient beings contravene this fundamental clarity, although they act all day long, they do not realize it themselves and wrongly enter the various realms of existence.

Those who must receive salvation are those for whom Amitābha Buddha, having realized the source, mobilizes compassion identical in essence with theirs, while sentient beings, strong in their delusion, undergo various illusory sufferings."
Compassion and suffering face one another; thus, the Way of resonance and response intermingles. Therefore, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says:
"The Tathāgatas of the ten directions cherish sentient beings as a mother remembers her child. If the child has fled far away, though the mother remembers him, what can she do?

But if the child remembers his mother just as the mother remembers him, then when I now encounter this period of suffering and my mind desires liberation, I shall certainly merge with the compassionate essence of Amitābha. It is certain.
I have been rescued and delivered, like a person encountering peril who seeks powerful assistance and surely attains liberation.

My three minds are fully awakened and my single resolve hastens toward the West; I shall rely upon and follow [the Buddha] until the end of the future, praising him throughout kalpas as numerous as motes of dust.
The three minds are the "mind of sincere resolve," the "profound mind," and the "mind of dedication and aspiration" within the context of the highest grade of the highest birth.
Sincere resolve is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); the profound mind is Prajñā; and dedication is Liberation (*vimukti*).

These three minds are truly present within a single thought-moment. The three are entirely one, and while being one, they are three; therefore, it is called "perfectly arising. One resolve, and so forth.

As for this, a sutra states: "One should single-mindedly fix one's mindfulness on a single point and contemplate the western direction. It further says: "One should give rise to such contemplation, sitting upright and facing west.
If the mind is frequently distracted, samādhi will be difficult to achieve; if one contemplates with unwavering focus, rebirth [in the Pure Land] will be easily attained.
Regarding the phrase "until the end of the future": as extensively discussed in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the "end of the future" refers to the Land of Real Reward (*sambhoga-kāya*).
The nature of the Dharma is eternally abiding and remains without exception throughout the three periods of time. From this moment on, having encountered it, it shall extend through the future;
we resolve to personally receive it, never to regress. As for those who praise it throughout kalpas:

it is because Amitābha diligently sought the site of enlightenment over accumulated kalpas, realized the three bodies, and fully manifested the perfection of all myriad virtues. Even if the goddess Sarasvatī were to [praise them] for a billion kalpas...

The praise cannot be fully proclaimed even in its smallest part; it must be understood with clear discernment that both the one who praises and the object of praise are the Dharma-realm, pervading all of space.
When all sentient beings hear these verses, the Buddhas of the ten directions receive my hymn of praise.
Within a single word or sound, one expounds immeasurable meanings; in praising a single virtue of the Buddha, ten thousand virtues are universally encompassed.

The four types of eloquence are spread forth without touching the lips, and the eight qualities of voice sing in competition without falling into the trap of verbal expression. One attains sudden awakening to perfect penetration and turns the hearing back toward one's own nature.
Thus, whether one offers praise or does not offer praise, there is no difference between them.
End of the *Commentary on the Praise of Amitāyus Buddha*.
Recorded by Ze: Throughout my remaining life, I have drifted with the world; how could I have known there existed such a swift and direct Dharma-gate to the Land of Peaceful Nurturing?
In the past, while traveling along the Ganzi River, I encountered Xu Jian of Xuanxu, who was diligent in this Way. Consequently, I was inspired to exert myself;

from then on, my perspective shifted entirely, and I was startled into awakening. I took leave of worldly ties and resided at Dengguan on Cangzhou, where I have spent years recollecting and practicing the teachings, never daring to fall away day or night, remaining oblivious to the changes of cold and heat. Whenever there is a ritual...
I have first carefully recited the verses of praise by Master Dazhi. Subsequently, I obtained the commentary on this text by Master Zhu'an Du, whose phrasing and meaning are clear and lucid.
Fearing deeply that it might fall into oblivion, I respectfully solicit my fellow practitioners to carve these words onto printing blocks.
I vow that all who see or hear this shall aspire to the ultimate realization. Alas! The nature of the mind is inherently possessed by every person.
I dare ask you all: throughout the twelve periods of the day, what is the true face of this so-called "mind" and this so-called "nature"?
In the summer month of the first intercalary month of the year Xiwu of the Jiading era, the lay practitioner Lou Ze—whose Dharma name is Zhengyin—respectfully inscribed this colophon:
"In the past, during the Tang dynasty, although I saw that those who cultivated the Pure Land practice were numerous, I have long recited the words of praise by Vinaya Master Daizhi."
It was previously unknown that the Master Zhu’an had written a commentary. Now, while Master Yu was visiting, this text was incidentally discovered among his writings.

It is hoped that it will soon be carved onto printing blocks to propagate its transmission. Coincidentally, there were two monks, Juezhu and Jingguang, who had long been devoted to the Western Paradise.
Upon seeing this text, they were moved with deep appreciation and donated their own wealth to commission craftsmen to carve the blocks, vowing to [preserve it].
When every person clearly realizes the nature of mind-only, they immediately ascend to the precious land [of enlightenment].
This was respectfully recorded by the Dharma-transmitting bhikṣu Junrei at the western chamber of Pao-p'u-t'i (Ratnabodhi) in East Luo,
on the third day of the ninth month in the year of Yi-hai, the third year of Kenpō in Japan.
